docs.text: focus --> String [0..1] A specific subject or experimental unit in a Study, that data in the StudyResult object is about - e.g. a particular variant in a population allele frequency dataset like ExAC or gnomAD. Implementation Guidance * The 'focus' of a StudyResult is the what anchors selection of all data items and provenance information that it contains. This focus may be a single participant or subject of a study (e.g. one patient in a clinical study, or one allele in a population frequency analysis). It may be a study group defined as an experimental unit in the study (e.g. a specific treatment arm of a clinical study). Or it may be a variable defined as a unit of analysis in the study (e.g. 'exposure to nicotine' in an analysis correlating this variable with clinical outcomes). dataItems --> DataItem [*] One or more data items that are included in the StudyResult because it pertains to the 'focus' of the result. This can be data that directly describes this 'focus' (e.g. the population frequency of an allele focus), or be metadata about how data about the 'focus' were generated (e.g the quality measures for the sequencing run used to determine this allele frequency). Implementation Guidance * Any type of data item from a Study may be captured in a StudyResult - including raw experimental/observational data, derived calculations or quality measures, provenance information about how the data were generated in the study, or qualitative expert interpretations of the primary study data (e.g. the interpretation of a blood cholesterol value of 250 mg/dL as being 'high', or a Polyphen functional impact score of 0.115 as being 'deleterious'). * The model specifies use of a key-value based 'DataItem' object to capture the meaning and value of each type of data item captured in a given StudyResult. But in practice, profiles for specific StudyResult types may choose to define one or more specializations of the generic 'dataItems' property as named attributes. This makes the data more succinct and parsable, and allows specific constraints to be applied and validated for different data items. For example, a PopulaitonAlleleFrequencyStudyResult profile may define a named 'focusAlleleFrequency' attribute that is required, and a named 'focusAlleleCount' attribute that is optional - both of which conceptually specialize the core-im 'dataItems' property. Under this approach, the core 'dataItems' acts as a placeholder to seed such specializations, but is not used directly in StudyResult profiles. interpretation --> Coding [0..1] The outcome of an interpretation of lower-level data item(s) in a StudyResult, that express some broader conclusion or insight that was made (e.g. that data indicates a result to be is high, normal, or low). Implementation Guidance * This attribute allows basic interpretations / classifications to be included in a Study Result, such as binning a data item or items as being in or out of some normal range. sourceDataSet --> DataSet [*] A larger DataSet from which the content of the StudyResult was derived. Implementation Guidance * In most cases, a StudyResult will be generated using data from one source dataset - but it is possible multiple datasets related to a single study contain data about a particular focus that get collected into a single StudyResult instance. componentResult --> StudyResult [*] Another StudyResult comprised of data items about the same focus as its parent Result, but based on a more narrowly scoped analysis of the foundational data (e.g. an analysis based on data about a subset of the parent Results full study population). Implementation Guidance * This attribute allows data creators to break down a StudyResult into finer-grained StudyResult instances with a narrower scope. For example, a StudyResult about the frequency of an allele in a global population of individuals can be broken down into separate 'component' Results about distinct subpopulations of individuals in the source data (e.g. frequency of the allele in asian vs african subpopulations, or male vs female subgroups). studyGroup --> StudyGroup [0..1] A description of a specific group or population of subjects interrogated in the ResearchStudy that produced the data captured in the StudyResult. Implementation Guidance * For example, in a StudyResult holding allele frequency data, this attribute points to a StudyGroup object that describes characteristics of the population that the frequency data was generated from (e.g. 'East Asian', 'Female').

docs.text: isAbout --> String [*] An entity or concept in the world that the information entity describes/is about. Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * e.g. In the context of a Statement object, this attribute may be used to indicate entities/concepts it is about, in lieu of providing a more precise description of what the Statement asserts to be true using subject, predicate, object, and qualifier properties. e.g. the Statement that "BRCA2 c.8023A>G is pathogenic for Breast Cancer" might be annotated to be about the variant 'BRCA2 c.8023A>G', and the disease 'Breast Cancer'. contributions --> Contribution [*] Specific actions taken by an Agent toward the creation, modification, validation, or deprecation of an Information Entity. Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * This attribute holds one or more Contribution objects, which provide structured descriptions of a contribution made to the Information Entity by a particular agent. dateAuthored --> String [0..1] Indicates when the information content expressed in the Information Entity was generated. Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * The term 'authored' as used in the model refers to the generation of 'information content' in the abstract sense, as opposed to a concrete encoding of this information in a specific language or format. e.g. for a Statement, this attribute captures when the information content expressed in the Statement was first generated by an agent. Information about when a particular concrete encoding of this information was created (e.g. as row in a table, or object in a json document) would live in a RecordMetadata object attached to the Information Entity). specifiedBy --> String [*] A specification that describes all or part of the process that led to creation of the Information Entity. Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * Examples - an experimental protocol or data analysis specification that describe how data were generated, or an evidence interpretation guideline that describes steps taken to interpret data in making a variant pathogenicity classification. * Note that this attribute captures specific *instances* of specifications/methods (e.g. the specific electron microscopy method described in https://doi.org/10.1002/ cpz1.1045) - as opposed to reporting a *type* of method applied (e.g. "Transmission Electron Microscopy"). supportingMethods --> String [*] Specific methods that were executed to directly or indirectly support creation of the Information Entity. Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * These may include methods that directly produced the Information Entity, or upstream/accessory methods that indirectly support creation of the Information Entity - e.g. methods used to produce data that was interpreted as evidence to generate a Statement of knowledge. * This field captures terms representing specific INSTANCES of methods applied, vs the 'supportingMethodTypes' attribute which captures TYPES of methods used. supportingMethodTypes --> Coding [*] Types of methodological approaches that were executed to directly or indirectly support creation of the Information Entity. Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * This field captures terms representing TYPES of methods applied, vs the 'specifiedBy' or'supportingMethods' attributes which capture specific INSTANCES of methods used. These may include types of methods that directly produced the Information Entity, or upstream/accessory methods that indirectly support creation of the Information Entity * Implementers should define a relevant source or set of method type codes/terms to use here, based on the needs of the domain or application.' derivedFrom --> InformationEntity [*] Another Information Entity from which this Information Entity is derived, in whole or in part. Inherited from: InformationEntity reportedIn --> String [*] A document in which the Information Entity is reported. Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * This attribute is used specifically to reference documents/publications where the Information Entity is expressed or reported. For a Statement, this might be a publication where the authors express the statement in text. For a Data Item, this might be a publication with a table or figure that reports the value of the data. sources --> String [*] A document or other informtion resource in which the information entity, or evidence supporting it, is reported. Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * This attribute is more general than InformationEntity.reportedIn (which is used to references a Docuement that directly reports the infrormation), and Statement.hasEvidenceFromSources (which is used to reference resources that provided evidence used to generate the knowledge expressed in a Statement). It can be used to cover both cases, in situations where a data provider does not know which is the case, or does not wish to make the distinction. informationQuality --> Coding [0..1] A qualitative term indicating the scientific rigor or reliability with which the information was generated/collected. Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * This is typically based on the quality of design and execution of the study or curation activity that generated it (e.g. were relevant controls assessed to show instruments were working, were all samples taken care of and handled identically, are methods sound and well documented, etc.). * The quality of information is intrinsic to the information itself, and not to a particular application of the information (e.g. as evidence for making an Assertion) * The quality of information is one factor that goes into the confidence we have in the information''s veracity (i.e. that it is an accurate reflection of reality it intends to measure or describe). Other factors informing confidence may include who did it (we may just not trust some Agents), when (if data created 500 years ago, we may have less confidence in it), and for Assertions, the relevance and abundance of supporting evidence. * Implementers should define a relevant source of codes or terms to use here, based on the needs of the domain or application.' recordMetadata --> RecordMetadata [0..1] Provenance metadata about a specific concrete record of information as encoded/serialized in a particular data set or object (as opposed to provenance about the abstract information content the encoding carries). Inherited from: InformationEntity Implementation Guidance * This attribute holds a structured RecordMetadata objects, which can be used to capture when, how, and by whom a record serialization was generated or modified; what upstream resources it was derived or retrieved from; and record-level administrative information such as versioning and lifecycle status. id --> String [1] The 'logical' identifier of the entity in the system of record, e.g. a UUID. This 'id' is unique within a given system, but may or may not be globally unique outside the system. It is used within a system to reference one object from another. Inherited from: Entity Implementation Guidance * Note that it is common for implementers to create their own internal logical ids - typically a serially or randomly generated value like a UUID that is assigned to the data object as it is created in a system. But an implementer may choose to reuse an existing, globally unique id from an external system or authority for this purpose (e.g. an HGNC id for a Gene object) - as long as it is unique within the implementing system, and can be used to reference the identified object in this context. identifiers --> String [*] A globally-unique 'business' identifier or accession number for the real-world entity represented by a data object. These are typically assigned by an external system or authority, and used to connect entities and share content across different systems. Inherited from: Entity Implementation Guidance * Preferred values for this attribute are CURIEs or URIs - so the system that provisioned the identifier is clear. * A given real world entity - e.g. a genetic variant - may have many business identifiers defined by different systems, which can be captured in the "identifiers" property to indicate that they represent the same thing. type --> String [1] The name of the class that is instantiated by a data object representing the Entity. Inherited from: Entity Implementation Guidance * MUST be the label of a concrete class from the data model. label --> String [0..1] A primary name for the Entity. Inherited from: Entity alternativeLabels --> String [*] Alternative name(s) for the Entity. Inherited from: Entity description --> String [0..1] A free text description of the Entity. Inherited from: Entity extensions --> Extension [*] A list of extensions to the Entity, that allow for capture of information not directly supported by elements defined in the model. Information about when a particular concrete encoding of this information was created (e.g. as row in a table, or object in a json document) would live in a RecordMetadata object attached to the Information Entity). from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model status: Draft rank: 1000 alias: dateAuthored owner: StudyResult domain_of: - InformationEntity range: string required: false multivalued: false specifiedBy: name: specifiedBy description: A specification that describes all or part of the process that led to creation of the Information Entity. comments: - Examples - an experimental protocol or data analysis specification that describe how data were generated, or an evidence interpretation guideline that describes steps taken to interpret data in making a variant pathogenicity classification. - Note that this attribute captures specific *instances* of specifications/methods (e.g. the specific electron microscopy method described in https://doi.org/10.1002/ cpz1.1045) - as opposed to reporting a *type* of method applied (e.g. "Transmission Electron Microscopy"). from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model status: Draft rank: 1000 alias: specifiedBy owner: StudyResult domain_of: - InformationEntity - Activity range: string required: false multivalued: true supportingMethods: name: supportingMethods description: Specific methods that were executed to directly or indirectly support creation of the Information Entity. comments: - These may include methods that directly produced the Information Entity, or upstream/accessory methods that indirectly support creation of the Information Entity - e.g. methods used to produce data that was interpreted as evidence to generate a Statement of knowledge. - This field captures terms representing specific INSTANCES of methods applied, vs the 'supportingMethodTypes' attribute which captures TYPES of methods used. from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model status: Informative rank: 1000 alias: supportingMethods owner: StudyResult domain_of: - InformationEntity range: string required: false multivalued: true supportingMethodTypes: name: supportingMethodTypes description: Types of methodological approaches that were executed to directly or indirectly support creation of the Information Entity. comments: - This field captures terms representing TYPES of methods applied, vs the 'specifiedBy' or'supportingMethods' attributes which capture specific INSTANCES of methods used. These may include types of methods that directly produced the Information Entity, or upstream/accessory methods that indirectly support creation of the Information Entity - Implementers should define a relevant source or set of method type codes/terms to use here, based on the needs of the domain or application.' from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model status: Informative rank: 1000 alias: supportingMethodTypes owner: StudyResult domain_of: - InformationEntity range: Coding required: false multivalued: true derivedFrom: name: derivedFrom description: Another Information Entity from which this Information Entity is derived, in whole or in part. from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model status: Draft rank: 1000 alias: derivedFrom owner: StudyResult domain_of: - InformationEntity range: InformationEntity required: false multivalued: true reportedIn: name: reportedIn description: A document in which the Information Entity is reported. comments: - This attribute is used specifically to reference documents/publications where the Information Entity is expressed or reported. For a Statement, this might be a publication where the authors express the statement in text. For a Data Item, this might be a publication with a table or figure that reports the value of the data. from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model status: Draft rank: 1000 alias: reportedIn owner: StudyResult domain_of: - InformationEntity range: string required: false multivalued: true sources: name: sources description: A document or other informtion resource in which the information entity, or evidence supporting it, is reported. comments: - This attribute is more general than InformationEntity.reportedIn (which is used to references a Docuement that directly reports the infrormation), and Statement.hasEvidenceFromSources (which is used to reference resources that provided evidence used to generate the knowledge expressed in a Statement). It can be used to cover both cases, in situations where a data provider does not know which is the case, or does not wish to make the distinction. from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model status: Draft rank: 1000 alias: sources owner: StudyResult domain_of: - InformationEntity range: string required: false multivalued: true informationQuality: name: informationQuality description: A qualitative term indicating the scientific rigor or reliability with which the information was generated/collected. comments: - This is typically based on the quality of design and execution of the study or curation activity that generated it (e.g. were relevant controls assessed to show instruments were working, were all samples taken care of and handled identically, are methods sound and well documented, etc.). - The quality of information is intrinsic to the information itself, and not to a particular application of the information (e.g. as evidence for making an Assertion) - The quality of information is one factor that goes into the confidence we have in the information''s veracity (i.e. that it is an accurate reflection of reality it intends to measure or describe). docs.text: sepio-linkml SEPIO was first developed as an ontology by the Monarch Initiative to support standardized RDF representations of evidence and provenance across integrated genotype-phenotype datasets (the Scientific Evidence and Provenance Information Ontology). The ontological model has since been abstracted into a generic Core Information Model (IM) that can be implemented in any language or format. The Core IM is domain-agnostic, and able to represent assertions and their evidence and provenance of any kind. Application of SEPIO to a specific data set or use case requires defining a ‘Profile’ that extends/customizes the generic core model for a particular domain or application. The components of the SEPIO Framework include: A Domain Analysis Model (DAM) : an informal description of the domain we are modeling (scientific assertions and their evidence/provenance) A Core Information Model (IM) : defines data structures that can represent information about this domain (for any type of assertion and evidence). A 'Profiling' Methodology : Implementations extend the core model with domain-specific content to define a “SEPIO Profile” - a custom schema for a particular application or use case. Ontology Support : An ontological representation of the core model that can be used if desired to produce linked data with ontology-based semantics. The modeling framework-based approach addresses challenges posed by the diversity of types, levels of complexity, and use cases for evidence and provenance across knowledge domains and application - which means there is no ‘one-size-fits-all’ solution. A framework allows custom models built on a common semantic foundation can provide a base level of understanding and interoperability, without restricting expressivity. While this approach may not always support out-of-the-box interoperability across all communities of use, it can significantly lower barriers to aggregating, harmonizing, and operating across disparate data. The SEPIO Core-IM specified in this repository was written in a yaml format using the LinkML modeling language , and uses LinkML tooling to automatically generate formal json schema specification and Github pages web documentation found here.

docs.text: Slot: activityType The specific type of activity performed or role played by an agent in making the contribution (e.g. for a publication, agents may contribute as a primary author, editor, figure designer, data generator, etc. . Values of this property may be framed as activities or as contribution roles (e.g. using terms from the Contribution Role Ontology (CRO)). Comments Each implementation can define terms for the specific types of activities relevant to their use case/application. \n- Note that if the same Agent performed multiple types of activities in contributing to some artifact, they may all be captured in a single Contribution object. However, if data creators want to provide metadata specific to each activity (e.g. when or how each was performed), then a separate Contribution object should be created for each activity. docs.text: Slot: componentResult Another StudyResult comprised of data items about the same focus as its parent Result, but based on a more narrowly scoped analysis of the foundational data (e.g. an analysis based on data about a subset of the parent Results full study population). Comments This attribute allows data creators to break down a StudyResult into finer-grained StudyResult instances with a narrower scope. For example, a StudyResult about the frequency of an allele in a global population of individuals can be broken down into separate 'component' Results about distinct subpopulations of individuals in the source data (e.g. frequency of the allele in asian vs african subpopulations, or male vs female subgroups). docs.text: Slot: confidenceInterval A measure of the probability that a parameter of interest will fall within a defined range of values around a mean or other statistical calculation. Comments Confidence intervals reflect the degree of uncertainty in a sampling method. They may be bounded on one or both sides, and are computed for a designated confidence level (most often 95% or 99%.. For example, a Hazard Ratio of 0.47 might have a 95% confidence interval between 0.42 and 0.55, with a p-value of = 0.001. The DataItem used to represent a confidence interval will indicate what type of interval is reported (e.g. ''95% CI''), and will contain separate componentDataItems representing the upper and lower bounds of the interval (e.g. ''0.42'' and ''0.55'').' docs.text: Slot: dataItems One or more data items that are included in the StudyResult because it pertains to the 'focus' of the result. This can be data that directly describes this 'focus' (e.g. the population frequency of an allele focus), or be metadata about how data about the 'focus' were generated (e.g the quality measures for the sequencing run used to determine this allele frequency). Comments Any type of data item from a Study may be captured in a StudyResult - including raw experimental/observational data, derived calculations or quality measures, provenance information about how the data were generated in the study, or qualitative expert interpretations of the primary study data (e.g. the interpretation of a blood cholesterol value of 250 mg/dL as being 'high', or a Polyphen functional impact score of 0.115 as being 'deleterious'). The model specifies use of a key-value based 'DataItem' object to capture the meaning and value of each type of data item captured in a given StudyResult. But in practice, profiles for specific StudyResult types may choose to define one or more specializations of the generic 'dataItems' property as named attributes. This makes the data more succinct and parsable, and allows specific constraints to be applied and validated for different data items. For example, a PopulaitonAlleleFrequencyStudyResult profile may define a named 'focusAlleleFrequency' attribute that is required, and a named 'focusAlleleCount' attribute that is optional - both of which conceptually specialize the core-im 'dataItems' property. Under this approach, the core 'dataItems' acts as a placeholder to seed such specializations, but is not used directly in StudyResult profiles. docs.text: Slot: dateAuthored Indicates when the information content expressed in the Information Entity was generated. Comments The term 'authored' as used in the model refers to the generation of 'information content' in the abstract sense, as opposed to a concrete encoding of this information in a specific language or format. e.g. for a Statement, this attribute captures when the information content expressed in the Statement was first generated by an agent. Information about when a particular concrete encoding of this information was created (e.g. as row in a table, or object in a json document) would live in a RecordMetadata object attached to the Information Entity). docs.text: Slot: direction A term indicating whether the Statement supports, disputes, or remains neutral w.r.t. the validity of the Proposition it evaluates. Comments Statements put forth a Proposition that expresses some possible fact about the world, and may provide an assessment of this proposition's validity (i.e. how likely it is to be true or false based on evaluated evidence). The semantics of the Proposition are captured in the 'subject', 'predicate', 'object', and optional 'qualifier' attributes. An assessment of the Proposition's validity can be captured using 'direction', 'strength', and 'score' attributes. The 'direction' attribute is used to indicate whether the Statement's Proposition is supported by the agent's assessment (when evidence favors its validity), is disputed by the agent's assessment (when evidence argues against its validity), or remains neutral (when conflicting or insufficient evidence exists to assert one direction or the other). (Enumerated values = 'supports', 'disputes', 'neutral'). Comments The 'focus' of a StudyResult is the what anchors selection of all data items and provenance information that it contains. This focus may be a single participant or subject of a study (e.g. one patient in a clinical study, or one allele in a population frequency analysis). It may be a study group defined as an experimental unit in the study (e.g. a specific treatment arm of a clinical study). Or it may be a variable defined as a unit of analysis in the study (e.g. 'exposure to nicotine' in an analysis correlating this variable with clinical outcomes). docs.text: Slot: hasEvidence A piece of information that represents or contributes to an argument for or against the validity of the Proposition put forth in a Statement. This is a shortcut relation that links a Statement directly to a piece of evidence supporting it, bypassing the Evidence Line class when used data creators do not utilize an Evidence Line object. Comments Evidence is any information that is interpreted in assessing the truth of the proposition a Statement puts forth as true or false. A piece of information only becomes evidence when it is interpreted in this way. Different types of information entities can be used and cited as evidence, including direct observation or measurement data, derived statistical calculations, data tables or figures in a publication, conclusions/findings from a particular study, or prior assertions of knowledge that themselves are based on their own set of evidence. This is a shortcut relation that links a Statement directly to a piece of evidence supporting it, bypassing the Evidence Line class - to be used data creators cannot or do not wish to create an Evidence Line object. docs.text: Slot: hasEvidenceItems An individual piece of information that was evaluated as evidence in building the argument represented by an Evidence Line. Comments A given Evidence Line may be supported by one or many individual evidence items. What matters is that all evidence items in a given Evidence Line get collectively assessed and assigned direction and strength as a single argument for or against a target proposition. Different types and scales of information entity can serve as evidence (experimental measurements or observations, data tables or figures, images, prior assertions, etc.) Only when assessed as evidence do we consider the information to be an 'Evidence Item'. For example, a piece of population frequency data about BRCA2 c.8023A>G becomes an Evidence Item when it is assessed for the support it may offer for a target proposition (e.g. the prospect of the variant’s pathogenicity). docs.text: Slot: hasEvidenceLines An evidence-based argument that supports or disputes the validity of the proposition that a Statement assesses or puts forth as true. The strength and direction of this argument (whether it supports or disputes the proposition, and how strongly) is based on an interpretation of one or more pieces of information as evidence (i.e. 'Evidence Items). Comments Evidence Lines result from the interpretation of one or more pieces of information to build an argument for or against a particular Proposition. These arguments have direction (supporting / disputing) and strength (e.g. strong, moderate, weak) relative to the Proposition they are evaluated against. For example, ExaC allele counts and frequency calculations for the BRCA2 c.8023A>G variant in different populations may be collectively assessed to provide an argument of 'moderate' strength in 'support of ' a proposition that the variant is pathogenicity for breast cancer. Evidence Lines are useful in cases where a data provider wants to describe in detail how information was assessed as evidence to generate and score different arguments for or against a Statement''s proposition. Evidence Lines can be omitted if such information is not available or needed. docs.text: Slot: informationQuality A qualitative term indicating the scientific rigor or reliability with which the information was generated/collected. Comments This is typically based on the quality of design and execution of the study or curation activity that generated it (e.g. were relevant controls assessed to show instruments were working, were all samples taken care of and handled identically, are methods sound and well documented, etc.). The quality of information is intrinsic to the information itself, and not to a particular application of the information (e.g. as evidence for making an Assertion) The quality of information is one factor that goes into the confidence we have in the information''s veracity (i.e. that it is an accurate reflection of reality it intends to measure or describe). Other factors informing confidence may include who did it (we may just not trust some Agents), when (if data created 500 years ago, we may have less confidence in it), and for Assertions, the relevance and abundance of supporting evidence. Implementers should define a relevant source of codes or terms to use here, based on the needs of the domain or application.' A RecordMetadata object could be created that describes this upstream source record, including information about its submission to ClinVar. Depending on its implementation, a score may reflect how confident that agent is that the Proposition is true or false, or the strength of evidence they believe supports or disputes it. The 'score' attribute serves the same purpose as 'strength', but allows for a quantitative assessment based on a numerical score. docs.text: Slot: strength A term used to report the strength of a Proposition's assessment in the direction indicated (i.e. how strongly supported or disputed the Proposition is believed to be). Implementers may choose to frame a strength assessment in terms of how confident an agent is that the Proposition is true or false, or in terms of the strength of all evidence they believe supports or disputes it. Comments Statements put forth a Proposition that expresses some possible fact about the world, and may provide an assessment of this proposition's validity (i.e. how likely it is to be true or false based on evaluated evidence). The semantics of the Proposition are captured in the 'subject,' 'predicate', 'object', and optional 'qualifier' attributes. An assessment of the Proposition's validity can be captured using 'direction', 'strength', and 'score' attributes. The 'strength' attribute is used to report the strength of this assessment in the direction indicated. Strength can be framed as a level of confidence that the Proposition is true or false, or as a level of evidence that supports or disputes it. Data creators can define the permissible values for the 'strength' attribute to indicate which of these facets is being assessed (e.g. 'high confidence' vs 'low confidence', or 'strong evidence' vs 'weak evidence') - or they can choose values that don't commit to one or the other if they don't want to make the distinction (e.g. 'high' vs 'medium' vs 'low'). docs.text: Slot: subjectClassification A single term or phrase summarizing the outcome of direction and strength assessments of a Statement's proposition, in terms of a classification of its subject. docs.text: Slot: targetProposition The possible fact against which evidence items contained in an Evidence Line were collectively evaluated, in determining the overall strength and direction of support they provide. For example, in an ACMG Guideline-based assessment of variant pathogenicity, the support provided by distinct lines of evidence are assessed against a target proposition that some variant is pathogenic for a specific disease. Comments An example based on the ACMG Guidelines for germline variant pathogenicity interpretation: Consider a curator assessing the evidence provided by population frequency data for a specific variant based on the ACMG criteria. In order to assign a strength (e.g. moderate vs strong) and direction (supports vs disputes) to this data as evidence, there must be some 'target proposition' toward which the evidence is assessed - which in this cases is the proposition that the variant is pathogenic for the disease of interest. If the PM2 criteria is deemed 'met', this indicates that the population frequency evidence provides 'moderate' (strength) 'support' (direction) for this target proposition. docs.text: START HERE — SEPIO Requirements Collection This folder contains the resources you need to ask an AI agent to complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms for your biomedical knowledge project. The goal is to capture what your project currently represents and what it should support , with a clean separation between: current-state requirements , grounded strictly in a defined canonical source/dataset/distribution; and desired-state requirements , which may draw on a broader evidence base to capture a maximal, evidence-supported requirements set for later human review. At this stage, the agent should describe the project in its own terms rather than trying to choose SEPIO classes or properties. After you review and confirm the completed forms, a separate SEPIO requirements-to-model step can determine which SEPIO model elements are relevant, where current SEPIO provides only partial coverage, and where follow-up or model extensions may be needed. What is in this folder Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx — the empty workbook your agent should complete. Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md — detailed semantic and field-by-field instructions intended primarily for the AI agent. REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md — the ready-to-copy prompt for asking an AI agent to complete the forms. RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md — an optional prompt that asks an AI agent to discover, classify, and organize project resources and propose candidate scope statements. RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md — practical guidance for assembling and reviewing a Resource Inventory. PROJECT_SOURCE_CHECKLIST.md — a checklist for gathering useful project schemas, documentation, examples, and other evidence. Requirements_Collection_Overview.md — the comprehensive human-facing overview of the requirements-collection workflow. examples/example_scope_statement.md — examples of project scope statements. examples/example_completed_requirements_review.md — an example Requirements Review Memo. CONTENTS.md — a list of files included in this package. Process at a glance Define the scope. Decide exactly which canonical source(s) control current-state answers and which broader sources may inform desired-state requirements. Create a Resource Inventory. Identify the best evidence, examples, versions, conflicts, and candidate scope statements. Give the agent everything it needs and have it populate the Requirements Forms. Inspect the workbook and review memo. Resolve uncertainties and correct anything that does not reflect the project. Move to SEPIO mapping. Once confirmed, use the requirements record as input to the separate requirements-to-model workflow. Step 1 — Define the Scope Statement Before the requirements agent starts, define a project scope statement . The scope statement is important because biomedical projects often have several different representations around them: internal curation data, canonical public distributions, intermediate pipeline artifacts, alternate releases, APIs, downstream knowledge graphs, and user-interface representations. The scope statement tells the agent which of these resources control current-state answers and which additional resources may inform desired-state answers . Minimal vs maximal scope A minimal scope describes only the canonical source/dataset/distribution selected for the review. Example: Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx , version 1.3.0. Current-state and desired-state requirements should both be limited to information represented in this canonical distribution. This produces a conservative requirements record describing that specific distribution. A maximal scope still defines a strict canonical source set for current state, but allows a broader evidence base for desired-state requirements. Example: Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx , version 1.3.0. Current-state answers must be based only on this distribution. Desired-state evidence: additional MeDIC-maintained intermediate curation artifacts, alternate distributions, the MeDIC paper and project documentation, and explicit project requirements may be used to identify a broader, evidence-supported desired-state requirements set. Where desired state differs from current state, the supporting source must be named in Explanation / Considerations . This keeps the current-state answers reproducible while allowing the first-pass desired-state requirements to be intentionally broad. A human reviewer can later narrow that maximal set. How to create the scope statement If the appropriate scope is already obvious, write it yourself. If not, use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md . The resource-discovery agent will propose: a minimal / canonical-distribution-only scope; a maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state scope; additional alternatives when justified; a recommended scope. Review or refine one of those candidate statements, then paste the finished scope statement into the SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE section of REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md . If the project has genuinely different canonical products with different evidence/provenance behavior, consider completing separate requirements reviews. Step 2 — Create a Resource Inventory A Resource Inventory is a structured list of the project materials that can support the requirements review. It is useful because it tells the requirements agent: which resources are canonical for current state; which additional resources may inform desired state; which examples to inspect; which sources are historical, upstream, downstream, or context only; which versions should be used; what conflicts or uncertainties exist; what the agent should retrieve itself versus what a human may need to provide. You can assemble the inventory yourself, or use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md to have an AI agent take a first pass. If you use the agent-generated inventory, review its source roles, versions, proposed scopes, and exclusions before proceeding. For detailed instructions, source categories, examples, and inventory structure, see: RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md Step 3 — Give the Agent Everything It Needs and Have It Populate the Requirements Forms Give the requirements agent: REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md (edited to include a PROJECT NAME and SCOPE STATEMENT) Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx (may be referenced in PROMPT or uploaded with PROMPT) Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md (may be referenced in PROMPT or uploaded with PROMPT) A [PROJECT]_Resource_Inventory.md file (upload with prompt) (optional) any additional private/local project files or datasets that the inventory identified as necessary (upload with PROMPT) Once these materials are provided, ask the agent to complete the forms using REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md . The agent should follow these principles: Current-state answers must come only from the canonical source set named in the selected scope. Desired-state answers may use the broader evidence set allowed by the selected scope. Desired state should be maximal but evidence-supported , not speculative. When desired state differs from current state, the agent should say what source supports the broader requirement in Explanation / Considerations . The agent should distinguish: canonical project data from upstream or downstream representations; current representation from desired capability; evidence items from evidence interpretation; evidence strength from confidence in extraction/alignment; stored provenance from process documentation. If the available information does not support a confident answer, the agent should use M / Maybe / Needs discussion or otherwise flag uncertainty rather than guessing. The agent should not use SEPIO mappings to decide what the project requirements are. Requirements come first; mapping comes later. Step 4 — Inspect the Deliverables The requirements agent should return two main deliverables. 1. Completed Requirements Workbook The completed workbook should preserve the original template formatting and contain the project's current-state and desired-state responses. The filename should include project name, version, date, and time, for example: MeDIC_Requirements_v0.2_20261013_1643.xlsx 2. Requirements Review Memo The memo should summarize: the selected project scope; the exact sources used for current-state answers; the broader sources used for desired-state answers; source versions/releases/commits where relevant; high-confidence conclusions; answers that need human review; conflicts, assumptions, and missing information; inaccessible resources, if any; observations about the forms/guidance; a small set of representative data examples. The memo should include: a few examples directly from the canonical current-state source; and a few broader/maximal examples from desired-state sources when they reveal additional requirements. Examples should be represented as close to the source structure as practical—for example, table rows for tabular data, JSON/YAML for structured documents, or triples/edges for graph data. What to review Focus especially on places where the agent had to interpret ambiguous evidence or infer desired-state intent. Ask: Did it assess the right canonical current-state source ? Did it use only that source set for current-state answers? Did it use the broader desired-state sources only where the selected scope allowed them? When current and desired state differ, did it identify the supporting desired-state source? Did it capture the major claim types ? Did it correctly identify what the project treats as evidence ? Did it distinguish evidence items from evidence interpretation? Did it capture provenance at the correct level? Did it avoid importing rich information that exists only in upstream sources unless the selected scope explicitly allows it as desired-state evidence? Did it avoid treating downstream API/display enrichments as canonical current-state requirements? Did it flag unsupported answers instead of guessing? Do the worksheets and memo tell a coherent story? Correct anything that does not accurately reflect the project. Once you are comfortable with the workbook, treat it as the confirmed project requirements input . Step 5 — What Can Happen Next The confirmed forms can then be passed into the separate SEPIO requirements-to-model workflow: Confirmed Requirements Forms + Requirement→SEPIO Mapping Registry + SEPIO source schema ↓ Requirements-to-Model Output Package That downstream package can include: Candidate SEPIO Covering Model Requirements Summary Requirements-to-Model Traceability Requirements Follow-Up & Modeling Decisions Gap & Extension Analysis Implementation Guidance Requirements Collection & Form Feedback Generation Manifest During the current pilot phase, an AI agent can generate these outputs with transparent provenance. Later, deterministic code can take over schema extraction, dependency closure, validation, traceability, and manifest generation. The project representative does not need to perform these mappings manually. Key principle Requirements first, SEPIO mapping second. The requirements-collection workflow should first answer: What does the selected canonical source currently represent, and what broader capabilities does the project evidence support as desired requirements? Only after those requirements are reviewed should the mapping workflow ask: How well does SEPIO represent those needs? More detailed guidance A more comprehensive overview of the workflow and tasks can be found in Requirements_Collection_Overview.md . Detailed guidance for building and reviewing the project evidence set can be found in RESOURCE_INVENTORY.md .

docs.text: This folder contains the resources you need to ask an AI agent to complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms for your biomedical knowledge project. The goal is to capture what your project currently represents and what it should support , with a clean separation between: current-state requirements , grounded strictly in a defined canonical source/dataset/distribution; and desired-state requirements , which may draw on a broader evidence base to capture a maximal, evidence-supported requirements set for later human review. At this stage, the agent should describe the project in its own terms rather than trying to choose SEPIO classes or properties. After you review and confirm the completed forms, a separate SEPIO requirements-to-model step can determine which SEPIO model elements are relevant, where current SEPIO provides only partial coverage, and where follow-up or model extensions may be needed.

docs.text: Before the requirements agent starts, define a project scope statement . The scope statement is important because biomedical projects often have several different representations around them: internal curation data, canonical public distributions, intermediate pipeline artifacts, alternate releases, APIs, downstream knowledge graphs, and user-interface representations. The scope statement tells the agent which of these resources control current-state answers and which additional resources may inform desired-state answers .
docs.title: Step 1 — Define the Scope Statement

docs.text: A minimal scope describes only the canonical source/dataset/distribution selected for the review. Example: Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx , version 1.3.0. Current-state and desired-state requirements should both be limited to information represented in this canonical distribution. This produces a conservative requirements record describing that specific distribution. A maximal scope still defines a strict canonical source set for current state, but allows a broader evidence base for desired-state requirements. Example: Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx , version 1.3.0. Current-state answers must be based only on this distribution. Desired-state evidence: additional MeDIC-maintained intermediate curation artifacts, alternate distributions, the MeDIC paper and project documentation, and explicit project requirements may be used to identify a broader, evidence-supported desired-state requirements set. Where desired state differs from current state, the supporting source must be named in Explanation / Considerations . This keeps the current-state answers reproducible while allowing the first-pass desired-state requirements to be intentionally broad. A human reviewer can later narrow that maximal set.
docs.title: Minimal vs maximal scope

docs.text: If the appropriate scope is already obvious, write it yourself. If not, use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md . The resource-discovery agent will propose: a minimal / canonical-distribution-only scope; a maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state scope; additional alternatives when justified; a recommended scope. Review or refine one of those candidate statements, then paste the finished scope statement into the SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE section of REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md . If the project has genuinely different canonical products with different evidence/provenance behavior, consider completing separate requirements reviews.

docs.text: A Resource Inventory is a structured list of the project materials that can support the requirements review. It is useful because it tells the requirements agent: which resources are canonical for current state; which additional resources may inform desired state; which examples to inspect; which sources are historical, upstream, downstream, or context only; which versions should be used; what conflicts or uncertainties exist; what the agent should retrieve itself versus what a human may need to provide. You can assemble the inventory yourself, or use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md to have an AI agent take a first pass. If you use the agent-generated inventory, review its source roles, versions, proposed scopes, and exclusions before proceeding. For detailed instructions, source categories, examples, and inventory structure, see: RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md

docs.text: Requirements Form Prompt — Complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms Use this prompt after the project evidence base has been reviewed and, ideally, after a Resource Inventory / Evidence Package has been prepared using RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md . The requirements workflow deliberately distinguishes current-state requirements from desired-state requirements : Current state is controlled by the canonical source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts named in the selected project scope statement. Desired state may be informed by a broader, evidence-supported set of project resources identified in the selected scope statement and Resource Inventory. This separation is intentional. The current-state columns should remain conservative and reproducible, while the desired-state columns may capture a broader maximal evidence-supported requirements set for later human review and refinement. Publicly accessible resources may be supplied as attachments, GitHub links, direct-download URLs, DOI/archive links, or version-pinned URLs. The agent should retrieve public resources itself whenever possible; human upload is a fallback. Copyable prompt Copy the prompt below into your AI agent's interface and replace the bracketed text. You are acting as a requirements analyst and as a knowledgeable representative of [PROJECT NAME]. Your task is to populate the SEPIO Requirements Forms workbook based on the selected project scope and the project materials and workflow resources I provide. PROJECT [PROJECT NAME] SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE [Paste the selected scope statement here. Prefer a scope statement produced by RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md and reviewed/selected/refined by the project representative.] The selected scope statement must identify, explicitly or by reference to the Resource Inventory: 1. CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET The exact source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts that control answers in the "Used in Current Data?" / current-state columns. 2. DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET The broader set of project resources that may be used to identify desired/future requirements. If the selected scope statement does not make these two source sets clear enough to apply reproducibly, stop and ask the project representative to clarify the scope before completing the forms. REQUIREMENTS-COLLECTION MATERIALS You will be provided access to the materials needed for this task. They may be supplied as: - files attached directly to this prompt; - public GitHub repository links; - direct-download URLs; - version-pinned GitHub URLs identifying a specific commit, tag, or release; - DOI/archive links; - other public project URLs or repository paths; - a reviewed Resource Inventory / Evidence Package produced using `RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md`- which may contain pointers/links to the types of resources above. The core requirements-collection materials are: 1. `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` 2. `Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md` A project Resource Inventory / Evidence Package should also be supplied when available. REQUIREMENTS MATERIAL LOCATIONS Requirements forms: [ATTACHMENT OR URL TO Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx] Instructions and guidance: [ATTACHMENT OR URL TO Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md] Resource inventory / evidence package, if available: [ATTACHMENT OR URL TO PROJECT_Resource_Inventory.md] Additional project materials, if any: [ATTACHMENTS, URLS, DOI LINKS, OR REPOSITORY PATHS] MATERIAL ACCESS RULES 1. If a public GitHub, DOI/archive, or other repository URL is provided, retrieve and use the referenced material directly. 2. For Markdown, YAML, JSON, CSV, text, schema, or similar files: - read the repository file directly when possible; - prefer the exact referenced version when the URL is version-pinned. 3. For `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` or any other binary spreadsheet: - retrieve/download the actual XLSX file; - do not rely on a rendered GitHub preview as a substitute for the workbook; - use the downloaded workbook itself as the template to populate. 4. If both a repository page URL and a direct/raw download URL are available for an XLSX file, prefer the direct downloadable file for workbook processing. 5. Do not require the project representative to manually download and re-upload a publicly accessible file unless you are unable to retrieve it yourself. 6. If a required file cannot be accessed: - identify the exact file/resource you could not retrieve; - provide the URL/path you attempted to use; - explain why the file is needed; - state whether the requirements review can proceed provisionally without it; - ask the project representative to upload that specific file only when necessary. 7. If a repository, DOI landing page, release page, or archive contains multiple plausible files, versions, or artifacts and the canonical one cannot be identified confidently, do not guess. Flag the ambiguity and ask for confirmation. VERSION AND REPRODUCIBILITY RULES 8. Prefer version-pinned URLs when they are provided. A version-pinned source may identify: - a Git commit; - a release tag; - a versioned release; - a DOI/archive version; - another immutable version identifier. 9. If a version-pinned URL is provided, treat that exact version as authoritative for this requirements run unless explicitly instructed otherwise. 10. If only a moving branch such as `main` or `master` is provided: - use the current version available at the time of the review; - record the repository path and, when possible, the commit SHA, release identifier, or retrieval date used; - do not silently substitute an older cached or historical version. 11. If both a version-pinned source and a newer unpinned source are supplied: - do not silently merge them; - follow the source-role rules in the selected scope statement; - record materially relevant differences. 12. Record enough source-version information in the Requirements Review Memo that another agent could reproduce the review later. RESOURCE INVENTORY / EVIDENCE PACKAGE 13. When a reviewed Resource Inventory / Evidence Package is supplied: - use the selected scope statement as the controlling rule for current-state and desired-state evidence; - use sources classified as CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL only for current-state answers unless the scope statement explicitly designates additional canonical companion artifacts; - use DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT sources only for desired-state reasoning, unless they are also designated CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL; - use REPRESENTATIVE EXAMPLES to verify actual data usage; - do not treat sources marked CONTEXT_ONLY / DO NOT TREAT AS CANONICAL as evidence of requirements; - preserve unresolved issues for human review rather than guessing. 14. If the Resource Inventory identifies public files that should be inspected during requirements elicitation, attempt to retrieve those files yourself before asking the project representative to upload them. 15. If the Resource Inventory and a directly inspected canonical source disagree: - the selected canonical current-state source controls the current-state answer; - flag the discrepancy; - do not silently alter the current-state answer based on a noncanonical source. 16. If the Resource Inventory identifies material that a human may need to provide, first determine whether you can retrieve it yourself. Human upload is a fallback, not the default. Use `Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md` to understand each form, question, controlled value, and response convention. CURRENT-STATE VS DESIRED-STATE RULES 17. Treat the two requirements columns as answering different questions. CURRENT STATE / F1: "What is represented in the canonical current-state source set selected for this review?" DESIRED STATE / F2: "What should the SEPIO-based representation support, based on the maximal evidence-supported project requirements allowed by the selected scope?" 18. Populate CURRENT STATE strictly from the selected CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET. Do not mark a requirement as currently represented merely because it appears in: - an intermediate curation artifact; - an earlier or alternate release; - a different distribution; - a paper or documentation page; - a roadmap; - an upstream source; - a downstream application; unless that resource is explicitly included in the selected current-state canonical source set. 19. Populate DESIRED STATE from the broader DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET permitted by the selected scope statement. This may include, when relevant and not explicitly out of scope: - explicit future requirements or roadmaps; - current project documentation and papers; - intermediate curation/analysis artifacts; - information captured elsewhere in the project's own pipeline but dropped from the canonical export; - alternate or earlier project distributions; - other project-maintained representations; - project examples, competency questions, or implementation guidance. 20. For the initial requirements pass, prefer a MAXIMAL EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED desired-state requirements set when the selected scope authorizes it. "Maximal" does NOT mean speculative. Every desired-state Y/M answer must be supported by project-specific evidence. The human reviewer may later narrow or remove desired-state requirements. 21. When a desired-state answer differs from the current-state answer, explicitly document the supporting source in the form's `Explanation / Considerations` field. When useful, classify the desired-state support using one of these labels: - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT A roadmap, issue, requirements document, competency question, or explicit statement says the project wants/needs the capability. - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT The project already captures or uses the information in an intermediate artifact, alternate distribution, curation workflow, analysis product, or other project-maintained representation, but it is absent from the selected canonical current-state distribution. - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT A paper, model/design document, curation guide, or other authoritative project documentation describes the capability as part of the intended project model or data product, even if it is absent from the selected canonical current-state source. Recommended explanation format when F1 and F2 differ: "Current state: [brief canonical-source observation]. Desired-state support: [SUPPORT TYPE] — [Source ID/title/version]: [brief evidence and rationale]." 22. If several desired-state sources support the same requirement, cite the strongest and most direct source(s) rather than listing everything. 23. A source that explicitly says a capability is out of scope, rejected, deprecated, or intentionally excluded should not be used to justify a desired-state requirement unless another authoritative source explicitly reverses that decision. IMPORTANT REQUIREMENTS-ELICITATION RULES 24. Answer the forms based on what this project actually represents or explicitly requires. Do not choose answers because they map conveniently to SEPIO. 25. Respect the selected project scope statement. Distinguish the scoped project/data product from: - upstream source systems; - internal systems outside scope; - downstream APIs; - user-interface/display enrichments; - derived products outside scope, unless explicitly admitted as desired-state evidence. 26. Distinguish: - information represented by the selected canonical current-state source; - information supported only as a desired-state requirement; - information available only in upstream sources; - information created or enriched only downstream; - process metadata that documents how data were generated but is not itself represented in the canonical source. 27. Use representative data/examples to confirm how the model is actually used, but do not infer a project-wide requirement from a single unusual record unless other evidence supports it. 28. Ground answers in supplied or discovered evidence. Distinguish what a source explicitly establishes from what you infer. 29. Do not invent missing requirements. If available project materials do not provide enough information to answer confidently: - use the form's uncertainty/review mechanism where available; - preserve the uncertainty; - flag the issue clearly for human review. 30. Preserve project-specific terminology and examples in explanatory fields where useful. 31. For each non-obvious answer, keep track of the source evidence that supports it so that the answer can be reviewed and traced back to its source. 32. Assess the project comprehensively across: - claim/assertion types; - claim representation structure; - semantic structure of reified claims; - evidence item types and representations; - evidence interpretation, grouping, direction, strength, and stacking; - provenance about information artifacts, agents, methods, processes, semantic alignment, encoding, and retrieval; - relationships between claim types and evidence types. 33. Do not use the Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry to decide what the project's requirements should be unless explicitly instructed to do so. Requirements elicitation must remain independent of current SEPIO coverage. 34. Do not proceed to Requirement→SEPIO mapping or generate a SEPIO covering model unless explicitly asked. WORKBOOK HANDLING RULES 35. Populate the provided `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` workbook itself rather than recreating the forms from scratch. 36. Preserve the workbook's existing visual formatting and structure, including: - sheet names; - row and column positions; - fills/shading; - fonts; - borders; - alignment; - word wrapping; - row heights; - column widths; - data validation; - other template formatting. 37. Change only the cells needed to enter project responses, explanations, examples, or explicitly requested review notes. 38. Do not redesign, restyle, normalize, or rebuild the workbook. 39. If technical limitations prevent safe editing of the workbook without altering its formatting, stop and report the limitation rather than silently rebuilding the workbook in a different style. 40. The returned XLSX should open normally in Excel without triggering a repair/recovery warning. Do not "fix" workbook internals by reconstructing the workbook if doing so changes the visible template formatting. If an Excel-integrity problem cannot be corrected without risking formatting changes, report it for human review. COMPLETENESS AND CONSISTENCY REVIEW 41. Before finalizing the workbook, perform a completeness and consistency pass: - check every applicable field; - compare answers across forms; - identify contradictions; - identify unanswered or weakly supported questions; - identify places where free text implies a requirement not captured by a structured response; - verify that every F1/current-state Y/M answer is supported by the selected current-state canonical source set; - verify that every broader F2/desired-state Y/M answer is supported by an allowed desired-state source; - verify that F1 and F2 were not conflated; - make sure upstream evidence/provenance capabilities were not incorrectly attributed to the canonical project source; - make sure process provenance described in documentation is not automatically treated as provenance stored in canonical records; - make sure downstream transformations are not treated as native current-state representation unless the selected scope says otherwise; - verify that the Explanation / Considerations field names the desired-state supporting source whenever F2 differs materially from F1. 42. Preserve unresolved issues rather than forcing a Y/N answer when the evidence supports uncertainty. DELIVERABLES A. Completed requirements workbook Return a completed copy of the supplied workbook. FILE NAMING: Use: [PROJECT]_Requirements_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].xlsx Example: MeDIC_Requirements_v0.2_20261013_1643.xlsx Use 24-hour/military time. Use `HHMM` without a colon for cross-platform filename compatibility. If a prior requirements version is supplied, increment or retain the version according to the project representative's instruction. If no version is specified, use `v0.1`. Preserve the original workbook formatting and structure. B. Requirements Review Memo Return a Markdown memo named: [PROJECT]_Requirements_Review_Memo_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].md The memo must contain: 1. Project scope used - reproduce or precisely summarize the selected scope statement; - explicitly identify the CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET; - explicitly identify the DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET. 2. Requirements-workflow materials used 3. Sources used for CURRENT-STATE requirements - list the exact datasets/distributions/schema artifacts that controlled F1/current-state responses; - record exact versions/releases/commits/DOI/archive versions/retrieval dates as applicable; - explain any explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts. 4. Sources used for DESIRED-STATE requirements - list the broader sources actually used to populate F2/desired-state responses; - group or annotate them where useful as: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT, EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT, DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT; - identify sources considered but excluded from desired-state reasoning and why. 5. High-confidence conclusions 6. Answers requiring human review 7. Apparent conflicts or missing information 8. Files/resources the agent was unable to access, if any 9. Form/guidance questions that were difficult to interpret 10. Important assumptions made 11. Project observations that suggest improvements to the requirements forms or guidance 12. Diverse representative data examples Include a small but diverse set of concrete examples that make the requirements tangible. Provide: - a few CURRENT-STATE examples directly from the selected canonical source set; and - a few broader/maximal DESIRED-STATE examples drawn from allowed desired-state sources when these reveal additional requirements. For each example, record: - Example ID - Current-state or desired-state example - Source ID/title/version - What requirement pattern it demonstrates Represent the example as close to its source representation as practical: - tabular/database source: show the example as a row/table with the original field/column names where possible. If a complete logical record is distributed across multiple tables, it is acceptable to denormalize the relevant fields into a single illustrative row, but label it as DENORMALIZED and identify the contributing source tables. - JSON/YAML document: show a compact JSON/YAML object preserving source field names and nesting. - RDF/graph data: show triples/quads/edge properties as appropriate. - free text/document source: show only the minimal relevant excerpt/fields necessary to demonstrate the requirement; do not reproduce unnecessary copyrighted text. - composite/maximal example assembled from several project sources: label it COMPOSITE/ILLUSTRATIVE, identify every contributing source, and do not present the assembled record as if it existed verbatim in one source. Do not fabricate values to make examples look complete. C. Source-access status Include a concise statement confirming: - which linked resources were successfully retrieved; - which attached files were used; - whether any fallback human uploads were required; - whether the review used version-pinned or moving-source URLs; - any public resources that could not be retrieved. Do not proceed to Requirement→SEPIO mapping or generate a SEPIO covering model unless I explicitly ask you to do so. docs.text: Use this prompt after the project evidence base has been reviewed and, ideally, after a Resource Inventory / Evidence Package has been prepared using RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md . The requirements workflow deliberately distinguishes current-state requirements from desired-state requirements : Current state is controlled by the canonical source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts named in the selected project scope statement. Desired state may be informed by a broader, evidence-supported set of project resources identified in the selected scope statement and Resource Inventory. This separation is intentional. The current-state columns should remain conservative and reproducible, while the desired-state columns may capture a broader maximal evidence-supported requirements set for later human review and refinement. Publicly accessible resources may be supplied as attachments, GitHub links, direct-download URLs, DOI/archive links, or version-pinned URLs. The agent should retrieve public resources itself whenever possible; human upload is a fallback.
