docs.text: Copy the prompt below into your AI agent's interface and replace the bracketed text. You are acting as a requirements analyst and as a knowledgeable representative of [PROJECT NAME]. Your task is to populate the SEPIO Requirements Forms workbook based on the selected project scope and the project materials and workflow resources I provide. PROJECT [PROJECT NAME] SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE [Paste the selected scope statement here. Prefer a scope statement produced by RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md and reviewed/selected/refined by the project representative.] The selected scope statement must identify, explicitly or by reference to the Resource Inventory: 1. CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET The exact source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts that control answers in the "Used in Current Data?" / current-state columns. 2. DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET The broader set of project resources that may be used to identify desired/future requirements. If the selected scope statement does not make these two source sets clear enough to apply reproducibly, stop and ask the project representative to clarify the scope before completing the forms. REQUIREMENTS-COLLECTION MATERIALS You will be provided access to the materials needed for this task. They may be supplied as: - files attached directly to this prompt; - public GitHub repository links; - direct-download URLs; - version-pinned GitHub URLs identifying a specific commit, tag, or release; - DOI/archive links; - other public project URLs or repository paths; - a reviewed Resource Inventory / Evidence Package produced using `RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md`- which may contain pointers/links to the types of resources above. The core requirements-collection materials are: 1. `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` 2. `Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md` A project Resource Inventory / Evidence Package should also be supplied when available. REQUIREMENTS MATERIAL LOCATIONS Requirements forms: [ATTACHMENT OR URL TO Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx] Instructions and guidance: [ATTACHMENT OR URL TO Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md] Resource inventory / evidence package, if available: [ATTACHMENT OR URL TO PROJECT_Resource_Inventory.md] Additional project materials, if any: [ATTACHMENTS, URLS, DOI LINKS, OR REPOSITORY PATHS] MATERIAL ACCESS RULES 1. If a public GitHub, DOI/archive, or other repository URL is provided, retrieve and use the referenced material directly. 2. For Markdown, YAML, JSON, CSV, text, schema, or similar files: - read the repository file directly when possible; - prefer the exact referenced version when the URL is version-pinned. 3. For `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` or any other binary spreadsheet: - retrieve/download the actual XLSX file; - do not rely on a rendered GitHub preview as a substitute for the workbook; - use the downloaded workbook itself as the template to populate. 4. If both a repository page URL and a direct/raw download URL are available for an XLSX file, prefer the direct downloadable file for workbook processing. 5. Do not require the project representative to manually download and re-upload a publicly accessible file unless you are unable to retrieve it yourself. 6. If a required file cannot be accessed: - identify the exact file/resource you could not retrieve; - provide the URL/path you attempted to use; - explain why the file is needed; - state whether the requirements review can proceed provisionally without it; - ask the project representative to upload that specific file only when necessary. 7. If a repository, DOI landing page, release page, or archive contains multiple plausible files, versions, or artifacts and the canonical one cannot be identified confidently, do not guess. Flag the ambiguity and ask for confirmation. VERSION AND REPRODUCIBILITY RULES 8. Prefer version-pinned URLs when they are provided. A version-pinned source may identify: - a Git commit; - a release tag; - a versioned release; - a DOI/archive version; - another immutable version identifier. 9. If a version-pinned URL is provided, treat that exact version as authoritative for this requirements run unless explicitly instructed otherwise. 10. If only a moving branch such as `main` or `master` is provided: - use the current version available at the time of the review; - record the repository path and, when possible, the commit SHA, release identifier, or retrieval date used; - do not silently substitute an older cached or historical version. 11. If both a version-pinned source and a newer unpinned source are supplied: - do not silently merge them; - follow the source-role rules in the selected scope statement; - record materially relevant differences. 12. Record enough source-version information in the Requirements Review Memo that another agent could reproduce the review later. RESOURCE INVENTORY / EVIDENCE PACKAGE 13. When a reviewed Resource Inventory / Evidence Package is supplied: - use the selected scope statement as the controlling rule for current-state and desired-state evidence; - use sources classified as CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL only for current-state answers unless the scope statement explicitly designates additional canonical companion artifacts; - use DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT sources only for desired-state reasoning, unless they are also designated CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL; - use REPRESENTATIVE EXAMPLES to verify actual data usage; - do not treat sources marked CONTEXT_ONLY / DO NOT TREAT AS CANONICAL as evidence of requirements; - preserve unresolved issues for human review rather than guessing. 14. If the Resource Inventory identifies public files that should be inspected during requirements elicitation, attempt to retrieve those files yourself before asking the project representative to upload them. 15. If the Resource Inventory and a directly inspected canonical source disagree: - the selected canonical current-state source controls the current-state answer; - flag the discrepancy; - do not silently alter the current-state answer based on a noncanonical source. 16. If the Resource Inventory identifies material that a human may need to provide, first determine whether you can retrieve it yourself. Human upload is a fallback, not the default. Use `Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md` to understand each form, question, controlled value, and response convention. CURRENT-STATE VS DESIRED-STATE RULES 17. Treat the two requirements columns as answering different questions. CURRENT STATE / F1: "What is represented in the canonical current-state source set selected for this review?" DESIRED STATE / F2: "What should the SEPIO-based representation support, based on the maximal evidence-supported project requirements allowed by the selected scope?" 18. Populate CURRENT STATE strictly from the selected CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET. Do not mark a requirement as currently represented merely because it appears in: - an intermediate curation artifact; - an earlier or alternate release; - a different distribution; - a paper or documentation page; - a roadmap; - an upstream source; - a downstream application; unless that resource is explicitly included in the selected current-state canonical source set. 19. Populate DESIRED STATE from the broader DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET permitted by the selected scope statement. This may include, when relevant and not explicitly out of scope: - explicit future requirements or roadmaps; - current project documentation and papers; - intermediate curation/analysis artifacts; - information captured elsewhere in the project's own pipeline but dropped from the canonical export; - alternate or earlier project distributions; - other project-maintained representations; - project examples, competency questions, or implementation guidance. 20. For the initial requirements pass, prefer a MAXIMAL EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED desired-state requirements set when the selected scope authorizes it. "Maximal" does NOT mean speculative. Every desired-state Y/M answer must be supported by project-specific evidence. The human reviewer may later narrow or remove desired-state requirements. 21. When a desired-state answer differs from the current-state answer, explicitly document the supporting source in the form's `Explanation / Considerations` field. When useful, classify the desired-state support using one of these labels: - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT A roadmap, issue, requirements document, competency question, or explicit statement says the project wants/needs the capability. - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT The project already captures or uses the information in an intermediate artifact, alternate distribution, curation workflow, analysis product, or other project-maintained representation, but it is absent from the selected canonical current-state distribution. - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT A paper, model/design document, curation guide, or other authoritative project documentation describes the capability as part of the intended project model or data product, even if it is absent from the selected canonical current-state source. Recommended explanation format when F1 and F2 differ: "Current state: [brief canonical-source observation]. Desired-state support: [SUPPORT TYPE] — [Source ID/title/version]: [brief evidence and rationale]." 22. If several desired-state sources support the same requirement, cite the strongest and most direct source(s) rather than listing everything. 23. A source that explicitly says a capability is out of scope, rejected, deprecated, or intentionally excluded should not be used to justify a desired-state requirement unless another authoritative source explicitly reverses that decision. IMPORTANT REQUIREMENTS-ELICITATION RULES 24. Answer the forms based on what this project actually represents or explicitly requires. Do not choose answers because they map conveniently to SEPIO. 25. Respect the selected project scope statement. Distinguish the scoped project/data product from: - upstream source systems; - internal systems outside scope; - downstream APIs; - user-interface/display enrichments; - derived products outside scope, unless explicitly admitted as desired-state evidence. 26. Distinguish: - information represented by the selected canonical current-state source; - information supported only as a desired-state requirement; - information available only in upstream sources; - information created or enriched only downstream; - process metadata that documents how data were generated but is not itself represented in the canonical source. 27. Use representative data/examples to confirm how the model is actually used, but do not infer a project-wide requirement from a single unusual record unless other evidence supports it. 28. Ground answers in supplied or discovered evidence. Distinguish what a source explicitly establishes from what you infer. 29. Do not invent missing requirements. If available project materials do not provide enough information to answer confidently: - use the form's uncertainty/review mechanism where available; - preserve the uncertainty; - flag the issue clearly for human review. 30. Preserve project-specific terminology and examples in explanatory fields where useful. 31. For each non-obvious answer, keep track of the source evidence that supports it so that the answer can be reviewed and traced back to its source. 32. Assess the project comprehensively across: - claim/assertion types; - claim representation structure; - semantic structure of reified claims; - evidence item types and representations; - evidence interpretation, grouping, direction, strength, and stacking; - provenance about information artifacts, agents, methods, processes, semantic alignment, encoding, and retrieval; - relationships between claim types and evidence types. 33. Do not use the Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry to decide what the project's requirements should be unless explicitly instructed to do so. Requirements elicitation must remain independent of current SEPIO coverage. 34. Do not proceed to Requirement→SEPIO mapping or generate a SEPIO covering model unless explicitly asked. WORKBOOK HANDLING RULES 35. Populate the provided `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` workbook itself rather than recreating the forms from scratch. 36. Preserve the workbook's existing visual formatting and structure, including: - sheet names; - row and column positions; - fills/shading; - fonts; - borders; - alignment; - word wrapping; - row heights; - column widths; - data validation; - other template formatting. 37. Change only the cells needed to enter project responses, explanations, examples, or explicitly requested review notes. 38. Do not redesign, restyle, normalize, or rebuild the workbook. 39. If technical limitations prevent safe editing of the workbook without altering its formatting, stop and report the limitation rather than silently rebuilding the workbook in a different style. 40. The returned XLSX should open normally in Excel without triggering a repair/recovery warning. Do not "fix" workbook internals by reconstructing the workbook if doing so changes the visible template formatting. If an Excel-integrity problem cannot be corrected without risking formatting changes, report it for human review. COMPLETENESS AND CONSISTENCY REVIEW 41. Before finalizing the workbook, perform a completeness and consistency pass: - check every applicable field; - compare answers across forms; - identify contradictions; - identify unanswered or weakly supported questions; - identify places where free text implies a requirement not captured by a structured response; - verify that every F1/current-state Y/M answer is supported by the selected current-state canonical source set; - verify that every broader F2/desired-state Y/M answer is supported by an allowed desired-state source; - verify that F1 and F2 were not conflated; - make sure upstream evidence/provenance capabilities were not incorrectly attributed to the canonical project source; - make sure process provenance described in documentation is not automatically treated as provenance stored in canonical records; - make sure downstream transformations are not treated as native current-state representation unless the selected scope says otherwise; - verify that the Explanation / Considerations field names the desired-state supporting source whenever F2 differs materially from F1. 42. Preserve unresolved issues rather than forcing a Y/N answer when the evidence supports uncertainty. DELIVERABLES A. Completed requirements workbook Return a completed copy of the supplied workbook. FILE NAMING: Use: [PROJECT]_Requirements_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].xlsx Example: MeDIC_Requirements_v0.2_20261013_1643.xlsx Use 24-hour/military time. Use `HHMM` without a colon for cross-platform filename compatibility. If a prior requirements version is supplied, increment or retain the version according to the project representative's instruction. If no version is specified, use `v0.1`. Preserve the original workbook formatting and structure. B. Requirements Review Memo Return a Markdown memo named: [PROJECT]_Requirements_Review_Memo_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].md The memo must contain: 1. Project scope used - reproduce or precisely summarize the selected scope statement; - explicitly identify the CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET; - explicitly identify the DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET. 2. Requirements-workflow materials used 3. Sources used for CURRENT-STATE requirements - list the exact datasets/distributions/schema artifacts that controlled F1/current-state responses; - record exact versions/releases/commits/DOI/archive versions/retrieval dates as applicable; - explain any explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts. 4. Sources used for DESIRED-STATE requirements - list the broader sources actually used to populate F2/desired-state responses; - group or annotate them where useful as: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT, EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT, DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT; - identify sources considered but excluded from desired-state reasoning and why. 5. High-confidence conclusions 6. Answers requiring human review 7. Apparent conflicts or missing information 8. Files/resources the agent was unable to access, if any 9. Form/guidance questions that were difficult to interpret 10. Important assumptions made 11. Project observations that suggest improvements to the requirements forms or guidance 12. Diverse representative data examples Include a small but diverse set of concrete examples that make the requirements tangible. Provide: - a few CURRENT-STATE examples directly from the selected canonical source set; and - a few broader/maximal DESIRED-STATE examples drawn from allowed desired-state sources when these reveal additional requirements. For each example, record: - Example ID - Current-state or desired-state example - Source ID/title/version - What requirement pattern it demonstrates Represent the example as close to its source representation as practical: - tabular/database source: show the example as a row/table with the original field/column names where possible. If a complete logical record is distributed across multiple tables, it is acceptable to denormalize the relevant fields into a single illustrative row, but label it as DENORMALIZED and identify the contributing source tables. - JSON/YAML document: show a compact JSON/YAML object preserving source field names and nesting. - RDF/graph data: show triples/quads/edge properties as appropriate. - free text/document source: show only the minimal relevant excerpt/fields necessary to demonstrate the requirement; do not reproduce unnecessary copyrighted text. - composite/maximal example assembled from several project sources: label it COMPOSITE/ILLUSTRATIVE, identify every contributing source, and do not present the assembled record as if it existed verbatim in one source. Do not fabricate values to make examples look complete. C. Source-access status Include a concise statement confirming: - which linked resources were successfully retrieved; - which attached files were used; - whether any fallback human uploads were required; - whether the review used version-pinned or moving-source URLs; - any public resources that could not be retrieved. Do not proceed to Requirement→SEPIO mapping or generate a SEPIO covering model unless I explicitly ask you to do so.

docs.text: Resource Inventory — Guidance for SEPIO Requirements Collection A Resource Inventory is the evidence package used to support a SEPIO requirements review. Its purpose is not merely to list project files. It should make clear: which exact source(s) control current-state requirements; which additional sources may inform desired-state requirements; which sources are context only; which versions/releases should be used; what examples best demonstrate the project semantics; what conflicts, missing information, or access issues remain. For many projects, the easiest way to create a first draft is to use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md . 1. Start with the canonical current-state source Identify the exact source, dataset, distribution, schema, or release that should control answers to: Used in Current Data? Examples: a specific version of indications.xlsx ; a current LinkML schema release plus designated canonical records; a particular KG build/export; a database schema plus one named production distribution. Prefer a version-pinned source when possible. If several artifacts must be interpreted together—for example a data table plus its canonical data dictionary—identify them as canonical companion artifacts . Do not automatically include intermediate files, alternate releases, upstream sources, downstream APIs, or papers in the current-state source set. 2. Identify sources that may inform desired state Desired-state requirements can use a broader project evidence base when the selected scope permits it. Useful sources may include: explicit requirements or roadmaps; current papers or model documentation; curation/evidence guidance; intermediate curation or analysis artifacts; fields captured in the pipeline but dropped from the canonical export; alternate or earlier project distributions; competency questions; implementation/design documents. When useful, classify these sources as: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT The project explicitly says it wants or needs the capability. Examples: - roadmap item; - GitHub issue; - requirements document; - approved competency question. EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT The project already captures or uses the information somewhere, but it is absent from the chosen canonical current-state distribution. Examples: - semantic-alignment intermediates retained in curation files but dropped from a final compact export; - provenance stored in an internal curation record but not emitted publicly. DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT Authoritative project documentation describes the capability as part of the intended model/product even though it is absent from the selected canonical distribution. Examples: - a current project paper describing qualifiers not present in the selected release; - a modeling guide describing intended evidence structures. Do not use a source to justify desired state if it explicitly says the feature is out of scope, rejected, or deprecated unless another authoritative source reverses that decision. 3. Gather representative examples Real examples are essential because schemas and documentation may not show how fields are actually used. Try to select a small but diverse set that covers important patterns, for example: a typical claim; a claim with qualifiers/context; a claim with a source/evidence reference; a claim with richer provenance; a record showing normalization or transformation; a case where information exists in an intermediate artifact but is dropped from the canonical export; an alternate distribution exposing a capability absent from the canonical one; an unusual but important edge case. Assign stable IDs such as E01, E02, E03. For each example, record: source; claim/record type; what requirement pattern it demonstrates; why it was selected. 4. Useful source categories Depending on the project, useful resources may include: Schemas and formal models LinkML JSON Schema SQL schemas SHACL UML/class models data dictionaries export specifications Canonical distributions release spreadsheets JSON/YAML datasets KGX/RDF exports database dumps versioned API payload specifications Documentation model overview README files architecture/design documents semantic conventions project papers Curation/evidence materials curation SOPs evidence classification rules scoring/confidence guidance interpretation guidelines review/approval workflows Pipeline/provenance materials ingest/transformation documentation normalization/grounding procedures intermediate curation artifacts source-attribution rules logs or intermediate outputs when they reveal intentionally retained project information Requirements/future intent roadmaps GitHub issues requirements documents user stories competency questions approved design proposals 5. Distinguish neighboring resources from project requirements Pay particular attention to resources that are nearby but not actually part of the scoped project. Examples: upstream source databases; regulatory documents from which the project extracts information; external ontologies used for normalization; downstream KGs; APIs or user interfaces that add derived information; historical or superseded releases. These may be useful for context, but they should not automatically control current-state answers. They may inform desired state only when the selected scope explicitly permits them and the evidence is genuinely project-specific. 6. Record versions and conflicts For every important resource, record: version; release; tag; commit SHA; DOI/archive version; retrieval date when no immutable version is available. If two resources disagree: identify the conflict; identify which source controls current state; state whether the other source may still inform desired state; do not silently merge the two. Example: Release v1.3 lacks qualifier fields, but the current project paper explicitly describes contextual hyperrelations. v1.3 controls current state; the paper may support desired state under a maximal scope. 7. Recommended Resource Inventory fields A useful inventory table includes: Source ID Name Type URL / repository path Version / release / commit Authority level Requirements role Desired-state support type Requirement dimensions supported Important directly observed facts Access status Retrieval / human-assistance guidance Notes / cautions Suggested requirements-role values: CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT CURRENT_AND_DESIRED CONTEXT_ONLY Suggested desired-state support values: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT N/A 8. Access and retrieval guidance The requirements agent should normally retrieve public resources itself. A human should need to intervene only when: public retrieval fails; authentication/private access is required; the file exists only locally; multiple plausible versions/files exist and the canonical one is unclear; the human must decide which scope/version is authoritative. When human help is needed, the inventory should say: exactly what file/resource is needed; why it matters; what question it will resolve; whether the requirements review can proceed provisionally without it. 9. Candidate scope statements A good Resource Inventory should end with candidate scope statements. At minimum: Minimal / canonical-distribution-only Use the canonical distribution as both the current-state and desired-state evidence base. Best when the goal is to describe one concrete release conservatively. Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state Use only the named canonical source(s) for current-state answers, but allow broader project evidence for desired-state requirements. Best when the goal is to discover the broadest evidence-supported requirements set before human review. Additional scopes may be useful for projects with multiple legitimate products or distributions. The project representative should review and select/refine one scope before final requirements completion. 10. Final handoff Before giving the inventory to the requirements agent, make sure it clearly answers: What controls current-state answers? What may inform desired-state answers? Which scope was selected? Which sources are context only? Which examples should the agent inspect? What versions should it use? What public resources should it retrieve itself? Is any human-provided material genuinely required? What important questions remain unresolved? If those questions are clear, the inventory is ready to accompany REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md .

docs.title: DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT

docs.text: Real examples are essential because schemas and documentation may not show how fields are actually used. Try to select a small but diverse set that covers important patterns, for example: a typical claim; a claim with qualifiers/context; a claim with a source/evidence reference; a claim with richer provenance; a record showing normalization or transformation; a case where information exists in an intermediate artifact but is dropped from the canonical export; an alternate distribution exposing a capability absent from the canonical one; an unusual but important edge case. Assign stable IDs such as E01, E02, E03. For each example, record: source; claim/record type; what requirement pattern it demonstrates; why it was selected.
docs.title: 3. Gather representative examples

docs.text: Depending on the project, useful resources may include:
docs.title: 4. Useful source categories

docs.text: LinkML JSON Schema SQL schemas SHACL UML/class models data dictionaries export specifications
docs.title: Schemas and formal models

docs.text: release spreadsheets JSON/YAML datasets KGX/RDF exports database dumps versioned API payload specifications
docs.title: Canonical distributions

docs.text: model overview README files architecture/design documents semantic conventions project papers
docs.title: Documentation

docs.text: curation SOPs evidence classification rules scoring/confidence guidance interpretation guidelines review/approval workflows
docs.title: Curation/evidence materials

docs.text: ingest/transformation documentation normalization/grounding procedures intermediate curation artifacts source-attribution rules logs or intermediate outputs when they reveal intentionally retained project information
docs.title: Pipeline/provenance materials

docs.text: roadmaps GitHub issues requirements documents user stories competency questions approved design proposals
docs.title: Requirements/future intent

docs.text: Pay particular attention to resources that are nearby but not actually part of the scoped project. Examples: upstream source databases; regulatory documents from which the project extracts information; external ontologies used for normalization; downstream KGs; APIs or user interfaces that add derived information; historical or superseded releases. These may be useful for context, but they should not automatically control current-state answers. They may inform desired state only when the selected scope explicitly permits them and the evidence is genuinely project-specific.
docs.title: 5. Distinguish neighboring resources from project requirements

docs.text: For every important resource, record: version; release; tag; commit SHA; DOI/archive version; retrieval date when no immutable version is available. If two resources disagree: identify the conflict; identify which source controls current state; state whether the other source may still inform desired state; do not silently merge the two. Example: Release v1.3 lacks qualifier fields, but the current project paper explicitly describes contextual hyperrelations. v1.3 controls current state; the paper may support desired state under a maximal scope.
docs.title: 6. Record versions and conflicts

docs.text: A useful inventory table includes: Source ID Name Type URL / repository path Version / release / commit Authority level Requirements role Desired-state support type Requirement dimensions supported Important directly observed facts Access status Retrieval / human-assistance guidance Notes / cautions Suggested requirements-role values: CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT CURRENT_AND_DESIRED CONTEXT_ONLY Suggested desired-state support values: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT N/A
docs.title: 7. Recommended Resource Inventory fields

docs.text: The requirements agent should normally retrieve public resources itself. A human should need to intervene only when: public retrieval fails; authentication/private access is required; the file exists only locally; multiple plausible versions/files exist and the canonical one is unclear; the human must decide which scope/version is authoritative. When human help is needed, the inventory should say: exactly what file/resource is needed; why it matters; what question it will resolve; whether the requirements review can proceed provisionally without it.
docs.title: 8. Access and retrieval guidance

docs.text: A good Resource Inventory should end with candidate scope statements. At minimum:
docs.title: 9. Candidate scope statements

docs.text: Use the canonical distribution as both the current-state and desired-state evidence base. Best when the goal is to describe one concrete release conservatively.
docs.title: Minimal / canonical-distribution-only

docs.text: Use only the named canonical source(s) for current-state answers, but allow broader project evidence for desired-state requirements. Best when the goal is to discover the broadest evidence-supported requirements set before human review. Additional scopes may be useful for projects with multiple legitimate products or distributions. The project representative should review and select/refine one scope before final requirements completion.
docs.title: Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state

docs.text: Before giving the inventory to the requirements agent, make sure it clearly answers: What controls current-state answers? What may inform desired-state answers? Which scope was selected? Which sources are context only? Which examples should the agent inspect? What versions should it use? What public resources should it retrieve itself? Is any human-provided material genuinely required? What important questions remain unresolved? If those questions are clear, the inventory is ready to accompany REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md .
docs.title: 10. Final handoff

docs.text: Resource Inventory Prompt Use this prompt as the preliminary evidence-discovery and scope-definition step before completing the SEPIO Requirements Forms when the authoritative project evidence base or appropriate requirements-review scope is not already obvious. The purpose of this task is to: identify, evaluate, and organize the project resources that can inform requirements elicitation; distinguish resources that should control current-state requirements from broader resources that may inform desired-state requirements; and only after the resource inventory has been assembled and source IDs assigned , propose one or more provisional project scope statements for human selection before the requirements forms are completed. The discovery agent should not complete the requirements forms and should not map requirements to SEPIO. Copyable prompt You are acting as a resource-discovery, scope-definition, and evidence-preparation agent for the SEPIO requirements-collection workflow. Your task is to identify, evaluate, and organize the best available resources for understanding the following project/data/model and then recommend one or more reasonable scopes for a subsequent requirements review. PROJECT [PROJECT NAME] INITIAL PROJECT CONTEXT / SCOPE NOTES [Optional. Insert any initial project description, known canonical distribution, exclusions, questions, or tentative scope notes from the project representative. If nothing is supplied, discover and propose the scope from the available project resources.] GOAL Assemble a proposed Resource Inventory / Evidence Package that another AI agent can later use to complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms accurately and reproducibly. Do not complete the requirements forms yet. Do not map project concepts to SEPIO yet. Do not infer project requirements from what SEPIO supports. A central output of this task is one or more PROVISIONAL SCOPE STATEMENTS that the project representative can review and select before requirements elicitation. IMPORTANT ORDER-OF-OPERATIONS RULE Do NOT author the final provisional scope statements before you have: 1. discovered the relevant project resources; 2. assigned each source a stable Source ID such as S01, S02, S03; 3. classified each source's authority and requirements role; 4. identified representative examples; 5. documented important source conflicts, ambiguities, version issues, and scope exclusions; and 6. identified the recommended current-state canonical source set and broader desired-state evidence set. The scope statements should be written AFTER the Resource Inventory and source classification are established so that they can refer to concrete resources by **Source ID + name/version**. Think of the workflow this way: RESOURCE DISCOVERY ↓ RESOURCE INVENTORY WITH SOURCE IDs ↓ SOURCE ROLE / AUTHORITY CLASSIFICATION ↓ RECOMMENDED CURRENT-STATE AND DESIRED-STATE SOURCE SETS ↓ PROVISIONAL SCOPE STATEMENTS ↓ HUMAN SCOPE SELECTION ↓ REQUIREMENTS FORM COMPLETION The Resource Inventory should make explicit: - which exact source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or companion artifacts should control CURRENT-STATE requirements answers; - which broader project resources may be used to identify DESIRED-STATE requirements; - what resources are context only and must not be used as requirements evidence; - which materials are publicly accessible and should normally be retrieved directly by the later requirements agent; - which materials, if any, require a human project representative to download, upload, or clarify. SCOPE-DESIGN PRINCIPLES 1. Separate current-state scope from desired-state scope. The subsequent requirements forms contain two distinct concepts: CURRENT STATE: What is represented in the selected canonical project source(s) for this review? DESIRED STATE: What should the SEPIO-based representation support, based on the broader, evidence-supported project requirements allowed by the selected scope? Do not assume the same source set must control both. 2. Every provisional scope statement must contain TWO EXPLICIT SUBSECTIONS. Each proposed scope must be structured with at least: ### Current-state canonical scope This subsection must state: - what project/data product is being assessed for current state; - the exact Source IDs + source names/versions that control current-state / F1 / "Used in Current Data?" answers; - any explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts; - what kinds of related resources are excluded from current-state reasoning. Use language such as: "Current-state/F1 answers must be based only on S05 — [source name/version] and S06 — [source name/version]. No other resource may change an F1 answer unless the scope is revised." The later requirements agent must strictly stick to this set for current-state answers. 3. Every provisional scope statement must also contain: ### Desired-state scope This subsection must state: - what broader project capabilities are in scope for desired-state/F2 requirements; - the exact Source IDs + source names/versions that may inform desired state; - whether each broader source is being used as: - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT - important exclusions from desired-state reasoning; - the rule that any F2 answer that differs from F1 must identify its supporting source in `Explanation / Considerations`. Use language such as: "Desired-state/F2 answers may additionally draw on S01 — [paper], S08 — [intermediate artifact], and S09 — [alignment/QC artifact] to identify a maximal, evidence-supported requirements set. When F2 differs from F1, the requirements agent must identify the supporting source and support type in `Explanation / Considerations`." 4. The CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET must be precise and reproducible. This is the exact set of source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts that the later requirements agent must use to populate current-state / "Used in Current Data?" columns. Examples: - one versioned `indications.xlsx` distribution; - one current LinkML schema release plus explicitly designated canonical example data; - one KG release artifact; - one database export and its required schema/data dictionary. Do not broaden current state simply because richer information exists elsewhere in the project. 5. The DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET may be broader. When relevant and not explicitly out of scope, desired-state evidence may include: - explicit future requirements or roadmaps; - current project/model documentation and papers; - intermediate curation/analysis artifacts; - data captured elsewhere in the project pipeline but dropped from the canonical export; - alternate or earlier project distributions; - other project-maintained representations; - competency questions; - curation guidance; - implementation/design documents. The purpose is to support an initial MAXIMAL EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED requirements set that a human reviewer can later narrow. "Maximal" does not mean speculative. Every desired-state capability must be supported by project-specific evidence. 6. Classify desired-state support where useful. Use these labels when characterizing why a noncanonical resource is informative for desired state: - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT A roadmap, issue, requirements document, competency question, or explicit statement says the project wants/needs the capability. - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT The project already captures or uses the information in an intermediate artifact, alternate distribution, curation workflow, analysis product, or other project-maintained representation, but it is absent from the proposed canonical current-state distribution. - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT A paper, model/design document, curation guide, or other authoritative project document describes the capability as part of the intended project model/data product, even if absent from the proposed canonical current-state source. 7. Do not use a source as desired-state evidence when it explicitly says the capability is out of scope, rejected, deprecated, or intentionally excluded, unless another authoritative project source explicitly reverses that decision. SOURCE-DISCOVERY RULES 8. Respect supplied project context and discover scope boundaries. Distinguish the scoped project/data product from: - upstream source databases; - internal systems that are outside scope; - downstream APIs; - user-interface/display enrichments; - unrelated derived exports; - historical/superseded project versions. For every source, consider whether it describes: - the canonical project/data model itself; - a candidate canonical current-state distribution; - an alternate or historical project representation; - an intermediate curation/analysis artifact; - an upstream source; - a downstream representation; - an implementation detail; - future/project intent. 9. Prefer current, authoritative sources, but do not discard older/alternate/intermediate project artifacts that may legitimately inform desired state. For CURRENT-STATE canonical-source recommendations, prioritize: a. current authoritative schema/data model; b. current canonical distribution/release; c. current authoritative data dictionary; d. current representative data/examples; e. explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts. For DESIRED-STATE evidence, also consider: f. current model/design documentation and papers; g. current curation/evidence/provenance guidance; h. current ingest/transformation/pipeline artifacts; i. explicit requirements, competency questions, roadmap documents, or issues; j. intermediate curation/analysis artifacts; k. alternate or earlier project distributions that expose project capabilities or intent. When sources conflict: - identify the conflict; - state which source should control current state; - explain whether the conflicting resource remains useful for desired-state evidence; - do not silently reconcile the difference. 10. Look for sources that can answer questions about: - the kinds of claims/associations/statements represented; - how claims are structurally packaged; - whether claims are represented as reified objects, direct graph edges, slot/value pairs, tabular records, or other forms; - how subject, relationship/predicate, object, and qualifiers are represented; - what kinds of evidence items are retained or referenced; - whether evidence items are represented locally, externally, or both; - whether evidence direction, strength, grouping, or higher-order synthesis is represented; - confidence or scoring information; - provenance about agents, methods, resources, dates, review, extraction, grounding, normalization, encoding, retrieval, or ingest; - what information is retained from upstream sources versus discarded or transformed; - what richer information is captured in intermediate project artifacts but lost in the canonical distribution; - current capabilities versus documented future/intended requirements. 11. Include representative data/examples. When possible, identify a small but diverse set of examples that covers the major claim and EPC patterns. Include examples from: - candidate canonical current-state sources; and - broader desired-state sources when they reveal additional project requirements. Prefer examples that collectively test different situations, such as: - a claim with publication or regulatory support; - a claim with structured evidence metadata; - a claim with qualifiers/context; - a claim with source/provenance but little explicit evidence; - a case where richer project-internal EPC is dropped from the canonical export; - a case involving normalization/transformation; - an alternate distribution exposing a capability absent from the canonical one; - any unusual but important pattern. Do not collect large datasets when a small representative sample will establish the relevant structure and semantics. Assign each representative example a stable ID such as E01, E02, E03. 12. Record precise source locations and source roles BEFORE writing the scope statements. Assign each source a stable ID such as S01, S02, S03. For each source, record: - Source ID - Source title/name - Source type - URL or repository path - Repository/release/tag/commit/version when available - Authority level - Requirements role - Desired-state support type, when applicable - Scope relevance - Requirement dimensions supported - Important directly observed facts - Access status - Whether the later requirements agent should retrieve it directly or human assistance may be required - Notes/cautions Use these authority labels where appropriate: - PRIMARY_AUTHORITATIVE - SUPPORTING_CURRENT - REPRESENTATIVE_EXAMPLE - HISTORICAL_BACKGROUND - OUT_OF_SCOPE_CONTEXT Use these REQUIREMENTS ROLE labels: - CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL - CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION - DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT - CURRENT_AND_DESIRED - CONTEXT_ONLY A source should receive CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL or CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION only if you recommend that the later requirements agent be allowed to use it for current-state answers under at least one proposed scope. 13. Capture directly observed facts from key sources. For each major authoritative source, record concise facts explicitly supported by the source. Examples: - "The canonical table contains subject ID, object ID, and a source-text field." - "The canonical record does not contain evidence-direction or evidence-strength fields." - "Intermediate curation records retain Name Resolver candidates and LLM QC outcomes, but the final export drops them." - "The project paper describes hyperrelations absent from the selected release." Distinguish these directly observed facts from interpretation. Use labels where helpful: - DIRECT - INFERRED - UNRESOLVED 14. Retrieve publicly accessible materials before asking the human to provide them. When a potentially important source is publicly accessible: - first attempt to access/download it yourself; - follow GitHub, DOI/archive, release, and direct-download links; - inspect actual files/artifacts when record-level or schema-level details matter. Human assistance is a fallback, not the default. 15. Identify inaccessible, ambiguous, or human-supplied materials precisely. Human intervention may be needed when: - the agent cannot access/download the resource; - authentication, institutional permission, or a private repository is required; - the source exists only locally/internally; - multiple plausible files/versions exist and the canonical one cannot be identified confidently; - the public copy is stale/incomplete and the representative may have a better copy; - a human decision is required to choose the canonical source/version or scope. If human assistance is needed: - identify the exact file/resource; - provide the URL/path when known; - explain why it matters; - state what question it is needed to answer; - state whether discovery/requirements elicitation can proceed provisionally without it; - tell the project representative exactly what to download, upload, or clarify. 16. Distinguish process documentation from stored project content. A project may document curation, extraction, review, normalization, mapping, evidence assessment, encoding, or transformation. For each such source, determine whether it shows: - information actually stored in the proposed canonical current-state source; - information captured elsewhere by the project but omitted from the canonical export; - only an implementation process with no evidence that its outputs are retained. This distinction is especially important for desired-state scope design. 17. Do not begin filling the SEPIO Requirements Forms until the Resource Inventory has been reviewed and one project scope statement has been selected, or the project representative explicitly authorizes the requirements agent to use the recommended scope. PROVISIONAL SCOPE STATEMENTS 18. Author provisional scope statements ONLY AFTER the Resource Inventory and recommended source sets have been completed. The scope statements should function as selections over the Resource Inventory. Do not write vague statements such as: "Use the current dataset and relevant documentation." Instead write: "Use S05 — `matrix_indication_list.xlsx`, v1.3.0 and S06 — `matrix_contraindication_list.xlsx`, v1.3.0 for current state. Desired state may additionally use S01 — MeDIC primary publication and S09 — FDA semantic-alignment/QC intermediates..." Every named resource should be identifiable from the Resource Inventory by Source ID and name/version. 19. At minimum, provide: SCOPE A — MINIMAL / CANONICAL-DISTRIBUTION-ONLY This scope should: - identify the narrowest defensible CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET; - restrict current-state answers to those canonical source(s); - normally restrict desired-state answers to the same canonical source(s), unless a small number of explicitly inseparable canonical companion artifacts are required; - produce a conservative requirements record describing the canonical distribution itself. Structure it as: ### Current-state canonical scope - Scope statement - Sources: Sxx — [name/version], Syy — [name/version] - Explicit exclusions ### Desired-state scope - Scope statement - Sources: usually the same source set for the minimal option - Explicit exclusions ### Strengths / tradeoffs 20. Also provide: SCOPE B — MAXIMAL / CANONICAL CURRENT STATE + BROAD DESIRED STATE This scope should: - identify the exact CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET; - require the later agent to use only that set for current-state/F1 answers; - identify a broader DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET; - allow desired-state/F2 answers to draw on project-specific evidence such as: - intermediate curation/analysis artifacts; - alternate/earlier project distributions; - other maintained project outputs; - authoritative papers/documentation; - curation/modeling guidance; - roadmaps/issues/explicit requirements; - aim for a maximal evidence-supported desired-state requirements set that the human reviewer can later whittle down; - require the requirements agent to name the desired-state supporting source in `Explanation / Considerations` whenever F2 differs from F1. Structure it as: ### Current-state canonical scope - Scope statement - Exact Source IDs + names/versions - Canonical companions, if any - Explicit exclusions - Rule that no noncanonical source may change F1 unless the scope is revised ### Desired-state scope - Scope statement - Exact Source IDs + names/versions - Desired-state support type for each broader source - Explicit exclusions - Rule that F2 differences must cite supporting source + support type in `Explanation / Considerations` ### Strengths / tradeoffs 21. If other reasonable project scopes emerge, provide additional alternatives such as: - CURRENT RELEASE + CURRENT PIPELINE ARTIFACTS; - CORE PRODUCT + DESIGNATED COMPANION DATASETS; - DOMAIN-SPECIFIC SUBSET; - STRICT HISTORICAL RELEASE; - CURRENT PRODUCT FAMILY / MULTI-DISTRIBUTION SCOPE. Every additional scope must use the same explicit two-part structure: ### Current-state canonical scope ### Desired-state scope 22. Recommend one scope. After presenting alternatives: - identify the scope you recommend for the initial requirements exercise; - explain why; - state the tradeoff between reproducibility/conservatism and broader requirements discovery. Unless project context argues otherwise, prefer recommending the MAXIMAL scope for the initial requirements pass because it preserves a strict canonical basis for current state while surfacing a broader evidence-supported desired-state requirements set for human review. DELIVERABLE Return a Markdown document named: [PROJECT_NAME]_Resource_Inventory.md IMPORTANT: Use the following section order. The Resource Inventory and source classification must appear BEFORE the provisional scope statements so that the scope can reference established Source IDs. A. Project context used Restate the supplied project context/scope notes and any important assumptions used during discovery. B. Resource inventory Provide a table with these columns: - Source ID - Name - Type - URL / repository path - Version / release / commit - Authority level - Requirements role - Desired-state support type - Requirement dimensions supported - Important directly observed facts - Access status - Retrieval / human-assistance guidance - Notes / cautions For Desired-state support type, use when applicable: - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT - N/A For Access status, use concise values where possible: - PUBLIC_ACCESSIBLE - PUBLIC_DOWNLOADABLE - ACCESS_NOT_VERIFIED - ACCESS_FAILED - AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED - PRIVATE_OR_LOCAL - CANONICAL_FILE_AMBIGUOUS For Retrieval / human-assistance guidance, use: - AGENT_RETRIEVE - HUMAN_PROVIDE_IF_AGENT_ACCESS_FAILS - HUMAN_PROVIDE_REQUIRED - HUMAN_CONFIRM_CANONICAL_VERSION - HUMAN_CONFIRM_SCOPE - CONTEXT_ONLY_NO_DOWNLOAD_NEEDED C. Representative data/examples List selected examples using stable IDs. For each: - Example ID - Current-state or desired-state example - Source ID + source name - Claim/record type - EPC/model pattern demonstrated - Why selected - Whether directly inspected or still needs retrieval Prefer examples from both: - canonical current-state sources; - broader desired-state sources that reveal additional requirements. D. Upstream/downstream/context resources that should NOT be treated as canonical requirements evidence List neighboring systems/resources that could cause scope confusion. Explain whether each is: - context only; - allowed only as desired-state evidence under a specific scope; - fully out of scope. E. Known source conflicts, ambiguities, or version concerns Document: - conflicting sources; - stale documentation; - unclear implementation behavior; - unresolved version questions; - differences between canonical distribution and richer intermediate/alternate representations; - uncertainty about which release/file is canonical. For each conflict: - state what controls current state; - state whether another source may still inform desired state. F. Recommended source sets Complete this section BEFORE authoring provisional scope statements. ### F1. Recommended current-state canonical source set Identify the exact sources that should control F1/current-state answers under the scope you expect to recommend. For each source: - provide Source ID + source name/version; - explain why it is canonical; - identify any canonical companion artifact that must be interpreted together with it; - state what it is allowed to establish for current state. ### F2. Recommended desired-state evidence set Identify broader sources that may inform F2/desired-state requirements under a maximal scope. For each: - provide Source ID + source name/version; - state why it is relevant; - assign one of: - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT - note limitations or caveats. ### F3. Sources excluded from requirements evidence List Source IDs that should remain context only or fully out of scope, with a brief reason. G. Provisional scope statements Now author the provisional scopes using the Resource Inventory IDs established above. ### Scope A — Minimal / canonical-distribution-only #### Current-state canonical scope Provide: - paste-ready scope text; - exact Source IDs + names/versions controlling F1; - canonical companions, if any; - explicit exclusions. #### Desired-state scope Provide: - paste-ready scope text; - exact Source IDs + names/versions controlling F2; - explicit exclusions. #### Strengths / tradeoffs ### Scope B — Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state #### Current-state canonical scope Provide: - paste-ready scope text; - exact Source IDs + names/versions controlling F1; - canonical companions, if any; - explicit exclusions; - explicit statement that noncanonical resources may not change F1 answers. #### Desired-state scope Provide: - paste-ready scope text; - exact Source IDs + names/versions allowed for F2; - desired-state support type for each broader source; - explicit exclusions; - explicit statement that whenever F2 differs from F1, the requirements agent must identify the supporting source + support type in `Explanation / Considerations`. #### Strengths / tradeoffs ### Additional reasonable scope alternatives Include only when justified. Use the same explicit two-part structure: - Current-state canonical scope - Desired-state scope ### Recommended scope State which scope you recommend and why. H. Materials the requirements agent should retrieve vs. materials a human may need to provide Start with this rule: The requirements-completion agent should first attempt to retrieve all publicly accessible materials itself. The project representative should not need to manually download and upload public resources merely because they are listed in the Resource Inventory. Then provide: ### H1. Materials the requirements agent should retrieve directly For each: - Source ID - exact resource/file - URL/path - why needed - what should be inspected ### H2. Materials a human may need to provide only if agent retrieval fails For each: - Source ID - exact resource - why it matters - what the human should upload if requested Do not ask the human to provide these preemptively. ### H3. Materials that genuinely require human provision or clarification List only resources that: - are private/local; - require authentication; - cannot be publicly accessed; - require a human canonical-version decision; - require a human scope-selection decision. If none: "None identified at this stage." I. Evidence gaps / unresolved questions For each unresolved question, indicate whether it: - can likely be resolved by retrieving a public source; - requires human-provided material; - requires a human semantic/project decision; - requires scope selection; - can remain unresolved during preliminary requirements elicitation. J. Recommended handoff for requirements elicitation End with a compact machine-readable block. Use this structure: RECOMMENDED SCOPE: - Scope B — Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCES: - S01: [name/version] - S02: [name/version] CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL COMPANIONS: - S03: [name/version] DESIRED-STATE SUPPORT SOURCES: - S04: EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT — [name/version] - S05: DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT — [name/version] - S06: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT — [name/version] REPRESENTATIVE EXAMPLES: - E01 - E02 - E03 CONTEXT ONLY / DO NOT USE AS REQUIREMENTS EVIDENCE: - S08 - S09 AGENT SHOULD RETRIEVE DURING REQUIREMENTS REVIEW: - S02: [specific file/artifact] - S04: [specific file/artifact] HUMAN PROVIDE ONLY IF AGENT RETRIEVAL FAILS: - S07: [specific file/artifact] HUMAN-PROVIDED MATERIAL REQUIRED: - NONE or - [specific resource and why] HUMAN CONFIRMATION REQUIRED: - Select/approve one provisional scope before final requirements completion - [other issue] UNRESOLVED: - [brief issue] HANDOFF INSTRUCTION: Use only CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCES and explicitly designated CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL COMPANIONS to populate F1/current-state requirements. Use the DESIRED-STATE SUPPORT SOURCES allowed by the selected scope to populate an evidence-supported maximal F2/desired-state requirements set. When F2 differs from F1, identify the supporting Source ID + source name and desired-state support type in the form's `Explanation / Considerations` field. Do not use CONTEXT ONLY sources as requirements evidence. Attempt to retrieve public resources before asking the project representative to upload them. Flag unresolved issues for human review rather than guessing. K. Short resource-discovery summary Conclude with 5–10 bullets summarizing: - the canonical model/data product identified; - the recommended current-state canonical source set; - the broader desired-state evidence set; - the recommended scope; - the main EPC patterns observed; - important scope exclusions; - critical source/version conflicts; - additional public materials the requirements agent should retrieve; - whether any material currently requires human provision; - whether the package is ready for scope selection and requirements elicitation. Human handoff principle The Resource Inventory should make the division of responsibility explicit: Public and accessible: the requirements agent retrieves it. Public but retrieval may fail: the human provides it only if the agent asks. Private/local/authenticated: the human provides access or uploads it. Canonical version ambiguous: the human decides which version is authoritative. Scope alternatives remain: the human selects/approves the scope before final requirements completion. Scope-selection principle The discovery agent proposes the scope; the project representative owns the scope decision. The important architectural rule is: The Resource Inventory defines the evidence catalog; the scope statement selects which catalog entries control current state and which may inform desired state. For most initial requirements exercises, the recommended default is: strict canonical current state + maximal evidence-supported desired state This gives the modeling workflow a conservative, reproducible account of what the selected canonical distribution represents today while exposing a broader set of project-supported capabilities for human review before SEPIO modeling. Relationship to the requirements-form workflow The completed [PROJECT_NAME]_Resource_Inventory.md is intended to be provided to the requirements-completion agent alongside: Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md the selected project scope statement any materials explicitly identified as genuinely requiring human provision The selected scope statement should be copied from or derived directly from the Resource Inventory and should preserve its Source IDs. The later requirements agent should attempt to retrieve all other publicly accessible resources itself. The Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry is intentionally not used during resource discovery or requirements elicitation.
